doc.title: Putter Smith interviewed by Monk Rowe, via Zoom, February 27, 2024

title: Beck session, Sonny and Cher era with Don Randi, and quitting studio work
summary: Smith explains a fluke recent recording with Beck via Smokey Hormel. He recounts moving to electric bass for studio work at Don Randi's suggestion in the mid-1960s, then quitting after a producer kept asking him to simplify a Cher date line.

story.theme_name: In the studio: making records, then and now
story.community_name: Session players on the hits: "I played on that record"

blocks.x: Well I’ll mark it over here. Your list of studio work includes everyone from Sonny & Cher to Beck if this list is correct. When was the last — do you remember first of all the last studio date, like showing up to play a part? When was the most recent one for you?

Well the thing with Beck was last year but that was a total fluke. I’m not in that business anymore at all, it was a total fluke. There was a country western swing player, guitar player, named Smokey Hormel and we met in New York, actually New Jersey, and I began going to see his gig in Red Hook. And I enjoyed it very much. And these guys were really good country & western players, and I mean really good you know, really good. And there’s a swinging bunch of guys you know. And I mean I’m not that kind of a player or anything like that. And so anyway Smokey called me up and he says, “I’m coming to L.A. and I’ve got this gig and I want you to play on it.” I said, “Man I don’t know any of that music.” He says, “I’ll send you a list, it’s all on YouTube.” “Okay, okay.” Because I like him so much, he was such a great guy. So I spent, you know some hours getting it together and went and did the gig and it was a lot of fun, a lot of fun. It was silly you know. I don’t mean it was silly, it wasn’t silly, it was real. It was real. But I mean I’m playing bluegrass kind of bass you know. Bluegrass kind of, you know like [scats] you know that, and I’m being real. I’m not being silly about it, you know I’m seriously playing it, you know, giving it my heart. And so anyway Smokey is a friend of Beck. And Beck came into the gig and he says, “I want you guys to record.” You know. So great, okay. So we went over to Beck and I made a fortune in one day. But before that my studio work, Sonny & Cher circa, that was in the middle-‘60s. And my dear old friend Don Randi, I was working with Don at this club six nights a week making $86 a week, had gotten married recently and had a second child. And six nights a week and we were very happy and everything. And then he said, “If you get an electric bass,” he says, “I can get you some recording work.” And I said, “Okay, fine” you know. “Cause you’re supporting a family” you know. But we were renting a three bedroom house for $75 a month. This was just a different world. And so I began doing all these dates and I was doing like five, sometimes five a week with all sorts of people. And you know all that kind of stuff. And I went into — one day after about three or four years of doing this I went into one date and it was for Cher, not Sonny and Cher, just Cher and it was — I can’t think of the guy’s name. One of his names was Gene, a writer. And he had “Up a Lazy River” written in real nice, James Jamerson kind of bass line you know like [scats]

You know nice, fun. And the producer goes, “Can you play it — make it a little simpler?” I said, “Oh okay.” So [scats]. He says, “Can you make it a little simpler?” [scats] He said, “Well can you make it a little simpler?” So I go to like the nastiest, dirtiest commercial and I go [scats]. He goes, “Yeah, that’s it.” And at that moment I decided this is not why I became a musician. This is not why I became a musician. And I just simply stopped hustling those kind of gigs and within three months I was totally out. You know. I was totally out. And that was fine, and then I began doing some really good big time work, and I mean more on my career. So I was doing really good, good work that I loved and everything, and then I got called to do that film. I guess you know about that right?
